- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.7) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment turns negative (≤ -0.3) and forecast remains high, apply downward pressure: subtract 3–5% from the forecast’s upper half.  
- After a strong upward move in history (e.g., >70% increase in 5d), model tends to overshoot — cap the next 3–5 days’ forecast at 10–15% below the peak.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (0.2–0.6) and forecast is trending down, add a 2–3% upward bias to avoid premature mean reversion.  
- When sentiment history shows repeated volatility (e.g., alternating +0.5 and -0.3), model overfits short-term noise — smooth 3-day moving average before forecasting.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome is consistently below forecast’s 10th percentile, apply a 5–8% downward correction to avoid overconfidence in long-term trends.  
- If sentiment is rising but price is falling, model often misreads sentiment — delay correction until sentiment stabilizes or crosses 0.5.  
- If forecast is above 75% of recent 5-day high, reduce by 10–15% unless sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.8) and volatility is low.  
- When sentiment is low (≤ 0.1) and forecast is high, treat as “false signal” — apply a 5–10% downward adjustment to avoid overreaction.  
- If forecast shows a sharp drop after a spike, and sentiment is still positive, assume momentum — don’t correct immediately; wait for 2–3 days before adjusting.
